title: Draupadi's swayamvara
hook: a brahmin rises from the crowd and walks toward the bow

segments.voice: Yesterday, Draupadi's swayamvara: Karna at the bow, one sentence, and a glance at the sun. Did you notice where you looked first? Day seven hundred forty-three.

The kings have failed. Karna has put down the bow. The arena goes quiet. And from the benches where the brahmins sit, a young man stands up, dressed like any other brahmin student. The brahmins around him start murmuring. Some are alarmed: where famous kings have failed, what's a brahmin going to do, except make the rest of us look foolish? Others look at him, at his arms and the way he carries himself, and say: let him go. Today, the bow finds its archer.
screen: `THE ARENA GOES QUIET.` → `A BRAHMIN STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: It's Arjuna, of course, in disguise. He walks up to the bow and stands before it. He walks around it, the text says, bows his head to Shiva, the giver of boons, and remembers Krishna. Then he picks it up. In a moment the bow is strung. He fits the arrows, shoots, and the mark falls to the ground, struck through the opening. The arena erupts. Flowers fall from the sky, the text says. There's music. Brahmins wave their cloths in the air. And Draupadi comes toward him with a garland, and places it on him. Now keep the disguise in view. Arjuna is supposed to be dead. He's just won, in front of all the gathered kings, as a nobody: a brahmin with no name. And that's what makes the kings furious. A brahmin has taken the prize, they say, and they rise to fight. Bhima tears a tree out of the ground, strips it, and stands beside his brother holding it like a club. Between them, they hold the kings off. What's striking in the telling is the order of things. Before Arjuna lifts the bow, he walks around it, and bows. The strength comes after the bowing. And the man the whole arena can't name is the very one Drupada had the bow made for.
screen: `HE WALKS AROUND THE BOW AND BOWS.` · `THE MARK FALLS.` · `DRAUPADI'S GARLAND.` · `THE KINGS RISE; BHIMA TAKES A TREE.`

segments.voice: Before Arjuna begins, he circles what's in front of him. Let the breath settle. Bring to mind something you'll do later today that asks something of you. See it slowly from every side, as if you were walking around it. If you pray, you can bow to it inwardly before you start. If you don't, let the circling be enough. The bell holds the time.
Draupadi's swayamvara. Today, a disguised archer walks around the bow, bows, strings it, and the mark falls.
Your line: Draupadi's swayamvara. Today, before one hard task, pause and walk around it once, in your mind or on your feet. Day seven hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Walking around something sacred to honor it, pradakshina, is part of Hindu worship: people walk around temple shrines, sacred trees and the wedding fire, keeping them on their right.

pairs: pulls up a tree to fight

fork.setup: you're Arjuna, hiding among the brahmins. everyone thinks you're dead, and every king has failed. what do you do?
options: stay hidden; winning could give you away.
stand up and walk to the bow.
fork.reveal: he stands, walks around the bow, bows, and strings it in a moment. the mark falls, and the kings rise in anger.

original.note: Sanskrit pradakṣiṇā: walking around something to honor it, keeping it on the right.

trapdoor: what you thought: the best archer just grabs the bow and shoots.
what it means: Arjuna walks around the bow and bows his head before he lifts it.
what a scholar hears: the text names Shiva, the giver of boons, and Krishna in that pause, before the bow is strung.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Swayamvara Parva (Arjuna rises among the brahmins; strings the bow and hits the mark; Draupadi's garland; the kings rise and Bhima uproots a tree)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: the brahmins' divided reaction; Arjuna walking around the bow, bowing to Shiva (Isana, the giver of boons) and remembering Krishna; flowers from the sky; brahmins waving their upper cloths; Draupadi with the garland.
Confirm that the kings' anger is framed as a brahmin taking the prize, and that Bhima uproots and strips a tree.
The text may not specify that Arjuna kept the bow on his right; the original-word note gives the general meaning of pradakshina, not a claim about this passage.
Krishna's recognition of the brothers is left for day 744.
Editor pass: 'the mightiest kings' and 'every king in the land' softened to what the scene shows (famous kings; all the gathered kings).
Audit pass: the review's question didn't match day 742's carry (where you look first when something closes on you); fixed.
